# Explicit near-Grünbaum common-contact rigidity

Let `d>=2`, let K be a d-dimensional convex body, let W be its volume,
and let g be its ordinary centroid. Write

`D=K-K`, `||v||_D=inf{r>=0:v in rD}`.

The centrally symmetric convex body D contains zero in its interior,
so this is a norm. It is covariant under every invertible affine
change of coordinates: the number `||y-g||_(K-K)` is affine invariant.
As usual `gamma_r=(r/(r+1))^r` for positive integer r.

## Theorem

Suppose a finite family of closed halfspaces has a common boundary
point y, covers all of `R^d`, and satisfies

`|K intersect H_i| <= tau W` for every i,

where `gamma_d<=tau<gamma_(d-1)`. Then y belongs to the interior of K
and

\[
 \boxed{\quad
 \|y-g\|_{K-K}
 \le\min\left\{1,
 \frac{d^2(\tau-\gamma_d)}{\gamma_{d-1}-\tau}\right\}.
 \quad}                                                     \tag{1}
\]

In particular, if `0<=epsilon<gamma_(d-1)-gamma_d`, a budget
`tau=gamma_d+epsilon` gives a completely explicit modulus tending
linearly to zero with epsilon. For example, if epsilon is at most half
the dimensional gap, the right side is at most

`2 d^2 epsilon/(gamma_(d-1)-gamma_d)`.

No conditioning of a chosen normal matrix, positive lower bound on its
balancing coefficients, general position, or smoothness is assumed.
The constants in (1) are not claimed optimal.

The sole dimension-drop dependency is the fully proved theorem in
`candidate f9c635ce5abe9f17`: if the common
boundary point of a full-space halfspace cover is outside the interior
of a convex body, some cover member has fraction at least gamma_(d-1).
The proof below derives all additional estimates explicitly.

## 1. A uniform upper bound on section density

Fix a nonzero linear functional ell and normalize it so that

`max_K ell-min_K ell=1`.

Let p be the probability density of ell(X), where X is uniform on K.
The coarea identity expresses p(t) as the `(d-1)`-dimensional section
volume divided by `W |ell|`. Here `|ell|` is the Euclidean norm of
its coefficient vector; the use of this norm is only to express
coarea, and cancels in the result.

For every section level t,

\[
                         p(t)\le d.                         \tag{2}
\]

Indeed, let A be the section of K at level t, and choose support points
of K at its minimum and maximum ell levels. The two cones with base A
and these respective vertices are contained in K by convexity, have
disjoint interiors, and their heights sum to `1/|ell|`. Their total
volume is `|A|_(d-1)/(d|ell|)`. It is at most W. This proves (2),
including endpoint sections and facets. A zero-area section gives the
same inequality trivially.

It follows that shifting a threshold downward by a nonnegative amount
a can increase its cap fraction by at most da. Thus, for all real b,a,

\[
 \mathbb P\{\ell(X)\ge b-a\}
 \le\mathbb P\{\ell(X)\ge b\}+d(a)_+ .                     \tag{3}
\]

When a is negative the new cap is a subset of the old one; otherwise
(3) follows by integrating (2) over the intervening interval. Ordinary
volume gives zero mass to all cutting hyperplanes.

## 2. A uniform lower bound on a centroid slab

With the same width normalization, put `m=ell(g)=E ell(X)`. Then

\[
                         p(m)\ge1.                          \tag{4}
\]

Here is a direct proof. The section Brunn–Minkowski inequality says
that `p^(1/(d-1))` is concave on the open projection interval.
Consequently p is positive and log-concave there. Its support interval
has length one, and (2) bounds p above. With `0 log 0=0`, convexity of
`s log s` and integration against Lebesgue measure on this unit interval
give

`integral p(t)log p(t)dt >= (integral p)log(integral p)=0`.

This integral is finite: p is bounded and `s log s` is bounded below
on `[0,d]`. The mean m lies strictly inside the support interval.
A supporting affine upper bound for the concave function log p at m
therefore exists. Integrating it against p gives

`log p(m)>=integral p(t)log p(t)dt>=0`,

which proves (4). This argument makes no differentiability assumption
on p. Values at support endpoints do not affect either integral.

Let `A=m-min_K ell>0`. Concavity of the section root, together with its
nonnegative endpoint limit, gives for `0<=s<A`

`p(m-s)>=p(m)(1-s/A)^(d-1)`.

Thus, for every `0<=a<=A`,

\[
 \begin{split}
 \mathbb P\{m-a\le\ell(X)\le m\}
 &\ge p(m)\frac A d\left[1-(1-a/A)^d\right]\\
 &\ge \frac a d .
 \end{split}                                                \tag{5}
\]

The last inequality uses (4) and `1-(1-r)^d>=r` on `[0,1]`.
At a=A the formula follows by monotone convergence. Closed versus open
slabs make no difference because the projection has a density.

Combining this with classical Grünbaum at g proves the useful
one-cap inequality

\[
 \boxed{\quad
 \frac{|K\cap\{\ell(x)\ge\ell(y)\}|}{W}
 \ge\gamma_d+\frac{\ell(g-y)}d
 \quad\text{if } y\in K\text{ and }\ell(g-y)\ge0.
 \quad}                                                     \tag{6}
\]

The hypothesis y in K ensures that the displacement a=ell(g-y) does
not exceed A. The slab below the centroid is disjoint up to a null
hyperplane from the through-centroid cap. This justifies adding their
two lower bounds in (6).

## 3. Quantitative conditioning of the cover

Write the given halfspaces as

`H_i={x:ell_i(x-y)>=0}`,

with every ell_i normalized to width one on K. Put

`Delta=gamma_(d-1)-tau>0`.

For every `v in boundary(K-K)`,

\[
                   \max_i\ell_i(v)\ge\frac{\Delta}{d}.
                                                               \tag{7}
\]

First, the external-contact theorem and the budget imply y in int K.
The point `y-v` is not in int K. Otherwise, since y belongs to K,
the vector v would belong to the open set `y-int K`, which is contained
in K-K; this would put v in the interior of K-K, contrary to its
choice.

Translate every cap by -v. The caps

`H_i'={x:ell_i(x-(y-v))>=0}`

still cover the full space and share the exterior-or-boundary contact
`y-v`. By (3), each has fraction at most

`tau+d max{0,max_i ell_i(v)}`.

The external-contact theorem forces this last expression to be at
least gamma_(d-1). Rearranging proves (7). In particular the maximum
in (7) is strictly positive. This estimates the covering normal
directions themselves; small coefficients in a positive dependence
cannot evade it.

Equivalently, if `D^circ={ell:ell(v)<=1 for all v in D}` is the polar
of the difference body, the finite convex hull of the normalized
normal functionals contains `(Delta/d)D^circ`. Indeed its support
function is `max_i ell_i(v)`, while the support function of D^circ is
`||v||_D`; positive homogeneity extends (7) to every vector v, and
support-function comparison is equivalent to convex-set containment.

## 4. Completion of the proof

If y=g, (1) is immediate. Otherwise put

`r=||g-y||_(K-K)>0`, `v=(g-y)/r in boundary(K-K)`.

By (7) there is an i with `ell_i(v)>=Delta/d`. Its nonnegative
centroid displacement is therefore

`ell_i(g-y)=r ell_i(v)>=r Delta/d`.

Apply (6) to this original cap and its assumed budget:

\[
 \tau\ge\gamma_d+\frac{\ell_i(g-y)}d
       \ge\gamma_d+\frac{r\Delta}{d^2}.
\]

This is the nontrivial estimate in (1). The other bound r<=1 follows
from g,y in K. It could be replaced by the strict r<1 here, because
both points are interior, but the displayed closed bound is simpler.

At tau=gamma_d the proof forces r=0, recovering exact centroid
rigidity without an equality classification for Grünbaum. As tau
approaches gamma_(d-1), this particular modulus degenerates, consistent
with the sharp external-contact examples. The result applies to an
arbitrary finite full-space cover, so in particular to every positive
balanced circuit, including ones whose normal matrices approach
singularity in Euclidean coordinates.

This is a continuous single-body contact-localization theorem. It
does not assert that a mixed-integer cap-cover optimizer has one common
contact, that contacts on different fibers agree, or that a selected
mixed-integer center satisfying OC has been constructed.
